analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain power plant upgrades from Clean Air Act modification review.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Air Act, a power plant or factory that makes a major change to its operations can count as a 'modification,' which triggers a permit review of the plant's air pollution before construction can go ahead. This bill would have written three broad categories out of that definition: energy efficiency projects, pollution control projects, and 'reliability' projects at power plants. Plant operators could then carry out those changes without pre-construction approval of their pollution impact. The bill never advanced past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of stationary sources of air pollution — chiefly electric utilities and industrial plants — who would have been able to undertake physical or operational changes in the three excluded categories without going through the Clean Air Act review that applies to modifications. The 'reliability project' definition covers any change that improves the electric system's ability to supply power or withstand disturbances, a very broad description [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Power plant and industrial facility operators

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clean Air Act's definition of 'modification' so that energy efficiency projects, pollution control projects, and reliability projects are excluded, removing them from the pre-approval process for construction or modification of stationary pollution sources [S3][S2].

For operators, this means an efficiency or reliability upgrade at a plant would no longer trigger the permit review that applies to a modification, avoiding delay and the possibility of new emissions limits being applied [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Communities downwind of power plants and industrial facilities, who lose the pre-construction check on how a changed plant would affect local air quality. If a facility qualifies an upgrade as a 'reliability project' or 'efficiency project,' the public does not get the permit review the modification rule otherwise provides [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near power plants and factories

drawbacks.text: The 'reliability project' exclusion is extremely broad: any project that improves the electric system's ability to supply power or withstand disturbances — including changes to a plant's method of operation — would be exempt from modification review, and determining whether an improvement counts would fall largely to the operator's own characterization of the project [S3].

The 'energy efficiency project' exclusion turns only on a lower maximum hourly carbon dioxide rate, while other regulated pollutants need only stay within existing permitted rates, meaning a project could lower CO2 while keeping emissions of other pollutants at their permitted maximums without any review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aims — making it easier to install pollution controls and efficiency upgrades — are modestly defensible, since a project that genuinely cuts emissions faces review that seems backward. But the exclusions are written broadly enough that a plant could route major operational changes through the 'reliability' or 'efficiency' categories and skip the pre-construction pollution review entirely, and the burden of that loss falls on air quality in nearby and downwind communities. On balance, the bill traded a real public safeguard for a broadly written industry exemption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action through the end of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on July 11, 2019, where it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5][S1].
That referral was the last action the bill ever received; the committee never reported it and the Senate never considered it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Clean Air Act's modification review remains intact, so communities near power plants kept the pre-construction pollution check the bill would have removed. Plant operators, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downwind communities, who kept existing air review

for.name: Rand Paul
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exclude energy efficiency, pollution control, and reliability projects from the Clean Air Act modification definition.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No partisan test occurred: the bill drew no cosponsors of either party and never reached the floor, so no vote reveals where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and industrial plant operators
industries.note: The bill would have removed these stationary pollution sources' changes in three broad categories from the pre-construction permit review that applies to modifications, letting them alter plants without the public emissions check. The industry gains regulatory relief, while the cost of skipped review falls on air quality near the plants.
